content: At the subgroup level, the maximum weekly food group level is calculated by multiplying the subgroup servings by the number of subgroups. Low energy levels are defined as the estimated energy requirement (EER) for girls at the lower end of the age range and at the 25th percentile for weight-for-age. Middle energy levels are the EER averaged for boys and girls at the midpoint of the age range and at the 50th percentile for weight-for-age. High energy levels are the EER for boys at the upper end of the age range and at the 75th percentile for weight-for-age. All model solutions required seven daily servings of breast milk, which provided approximately 63–64% of energy. Five daily servings of starchy staple foods were required per week, while the minimum for all other food groups was zero. The five main food groups are: 1) starchy staple foods, 2) fruits, 3) vegetables, 4) dairy, and 5) protein foods. The eight Infant and Young Child Feeding (IYCF) food groups are: 1) breast milk, 2) grains, roots, tubers, and plantains, 3) pulses (beans, peas, lentils), nuts, and seeds, 4) dairy products (milk, infant formula, yogurt, cheese), 5) flesh foods (meat, fish, poultry, organ meats), 6) eggs, 7) vitamin A-rich fruits and vegetables, and 8) other fruits and vegetables. Minimum dietary diversity is defined as consuming foods and beverages from at least five of the eight defined food groups during the previous day (WHO 2021). The modeled food patterns are weekly, while the dietary diversity indicator is based on a single day. Food groups were counted even when weekly quantities were small. For feasible models, the maximum subgroup servings were defined as seven daily servings per week, multiplied by the number of subgroups to yield the weekly food group level maximum. Liberal models allowed for larger quantities of each subgroup. Optifood modeling selected the minimum quantity of starchy staple foods per week, with whole grain breakfast cereals being the only subgroup selected. Fruits and added fats/oils were not selected for this age group, and dairy was included in only one of six model solutions. All models included vegetables and animal-source protein foods, with diversity in the selection of subgroups within these groups. Most models also included plant-source protein foods. Feasible best-case food patterns included the weekly maximum for vegetables at all three energy levels. At the high energy level, the weekly maximum for protein foods was also included. Subgroups such as dark green leafy vegetables and liver were selected at the maximum level in all six solutions, while small fish eaten with bones were selected in five solutions. Other subgroups, such as peppers/tomatoes, immature peas/beans, and soy foods, were selected in four solutions. Diversity was lower in liberalized models, where larger amounts of fewer subgroups were selected. Most solutions included three of the five main food groups and five to seven of the eight IYCF food groups. For non-breastfed children, added fats and oils were included in all model solutions. Protein foods were particularly low in the middle energy level solution, reflecting the secondary Optifood objective of minimizing protein once nutrient targets were met. This age group was the only one modeled where nuts/seeds were included in solutions.
